stem: A simple pendulum 1.0 m long has a period of 2.0 s when released from 4 degrees. Its bob is swapped for one twice as heavy and it is released from 8 degrees. What is the new period?

r1.text: The period depends only on length and g; mass and small amplitude do not change it.

r2.text: A bigger swing covers more distance, so it takes longer.

r3.text: A heavier bob has more inertia, so it swings more slowly.

calc: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) = 2 pi sqrt(1.0/9.8) = 2.0 s; L and g unchanged

stem: A pendulum 0.40 m long swings with a small amplitude. Its bob is replaced by one three times heavier and the string is lengthened to 1.60 m. By what factor does the period change?

r1.text: T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g): the period grows as the square root of length and does not depend on mass.

r2.text: A heavier bob takes longer to speed up, so the extra mass also raises the period.

r3.text: A longer string means a wider swing, and a wider swing always takes longer.

stem: A block on a spring oscillates between x = -A and x = +A. What is its acceleration at x = +A?

options.B: Zero, because the block is momentarily at rest
options.D: Zero, because the block is moving fastest there

r1.text: The restoring force F = -kx is largest at the largest displacement, so the acceleration is largest there.

r2.text: If the velocity is zero, the acceleration must be zero too.

r3.text: The block is fastest at the ends, so its speed is no longer changing there.

stem: A spring oscillator has total energy 8 mJ at amplitude 2 cm. The amplitude is increased to 4 cm on the same spring. What is the new total energy?

r1.text: E = (1/2) k A^2, so doubling A multiplies the energy by 4.

r2.text: Energy is proportional to amplitude, so it doubles.

r3.text: The energy is greatest at the ends, where the block moves fastest.

stem: A transverse wave travels along a string at 12 m/s with frequency 4 Hz. The source frequency is raised to 8 Hz; the tension is unchanged. What is the new wavelength?

r1.text: Tension and mass per length fix the speed; the source sets f, so lambda = v/f halves.

r2.text: Shaking faster pushes the wave along faster, so the wavelength stays the same.

r3.text: A more energetic shake makes the wave move faster.

stem: A red dot is painted on a horizontal rope carrying a transverse wave that moves to the right. How does the red dot move during one full period?

options.A: Up and down about its rest position, ending where it started
options.B: To the right by one wavelength
options.C: Up and down, returning to its start only after two periods
options.D: Up and down while drifting right with each crest

r1.text: Each particle does SHM in place; only the pattern travels along the rope.

r2.text: The wave carries the bits of rope along with it.

r3.text: A bigger wave would push the dot along faster.

stem: Tuning forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. How many beats per second are heard?

r1.text: Loudness peaks each time the waves come back into step, which happens |f1 - f2| times per second.

r2.text: The envelope has frequency (f1 - f2)/2, so that is the beat frequency.

r3.text: The two notes add, so their frequencies add.

stem: Fork X (300 Hz) and fork Y give 6 beats per second. Wax is stuck on Y, lowering its frequency, and the beats rise to 8 per second. What was Y's original frequency?

r1.text: Lowering Y increased the beats, so Y was already below 300 Hz: 300 - 6 = 294 Hz.

r2.text: Beats are half the frequency difference, so Y differs from X by 3 Hz.

r3.text: Where the two sounds cancel, sound energy is destroyed, so the wax only changes loudness.

calc: f_Y = 300 - 6 = 294 Hz; after wax f_Y = 292 Hz gives |300 - 292| = 8

stem: You stand 2.0 m in front of a plane mirror. How far are you from your image?

r1.text: The image is as far behind the mirror as you are in front: 2.0 m + 2.0 m.

r2.text: The image forms on the surface of the mirror.

r3.text: Moving back makes your image smaller so it fits closer to you.

stem: In a wall mirror you can see yourself from head to knees. You step 2 m further back. What do you now see?

r1.text: The ray from any part of you to your eye meets the mirror halfway up, whatever the distance, so the visible part does not change.

r2.text: Further away the image is smaller, so more of it fits in the mirror.

r3.text: The image sits on the glass, so stepping back changes nothing about it.

stem: An object stands 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Describe the image.

options.A: Virtual, erect, 3x magnified, 30 cm behind the mirror
options.B: Real, inverted, 3x magnified, 30 cm in front of the mirror
options.C: Virtual, erect, 0.6x size, 6 cm behind the mirror

r1.text: Inside the focal length the reflected rays diverge and only appear to meet behind the mirror: virtual and erect.

r2.text: A concave mirror always brings light to a real focus in front of it.

r3.text: A real image can form only where a screen catches it.

stem: A concave mirror forms a sharp real image of a candle on a screen. The screen is taken away. What happens to the image?

options.A: It still forms at the same place; an eye beyond that point can see it
options.B: It disappears, because a real image needs a screen
options.C: It moves to the focus of the mirror

r1.text: The reflected rays still cross at that point; the screen only scatters them so we can see them.

r2.text: Without a screen there is nothing for the image to form on.

r3.text: A concave mirror always makes a real image, wherever the light ends up.

stem: A convex lens forms a real image of an arrow on a screen. The top half of the lens is covered with black paper. What happens to the image?

options.A: The full image remains but is dimmer
options.B: Only the bottom half of the image remains
options.C: Only the top half of the image remains

r1.text: Every point of the object sends rays through every part of the lens, so the uncovered half still forms the whole image with less light.

r2.text: Each half of the lens makes its own half of the picture.

r3.text: Glass bends light away from the normal, so only the uncovered edge can send light to the screen.

stem: An object is 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image and what is it like?

options.A: 60 cm on the other side; real, inverted, 2x
options.B: 12 cm on the other side; real, inverted, 0.4x
options.C: 60 cm on the same side; virtual, erect, 2x
options.D: 20 cm on the other side, at the focus

r1.text: Using 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with u = -30 cm gives v = +60 cm: a real image on the far side.

r2.text: Glass bends light away from the normal, so a convex lens spreads rays out and the image is virtual.

r3.text: Each part of the lens images one part of the object, so the image size depends on how much lens is used.

stem: In a double-slit experiment the slit separation d is doubled; everything else stays the same. What happens to the fringe width?

r1.text: beta = lambda D / d, so doubling d halves beta.

r2.text: Slits further apart spread the pattern out more.

r3.text: Dark fringes are the shadows between the slits, so moving the slits apart moves the shadows apart.

stem: What is happening at the centre of a dark fringe in a double-slit pattern?

options.A: Waves from the two slits arrive half a wavelength out of step and cancel
options.B: No light from either slit reaches that point
options.C: Light from only one slit reaches that point
options.D: The light energy arriving there is destroyed

r1.text: A path difference of (n + 1/2) lambda makes the waves cancel; the energy is redistributed to the bright fringes.

r2.text: The slits cast shadows, and the dark fringes are those shadows.

r3.text: Where the waves cancel, their energy is lost.

stem: In a double-slit experiment, one slit is covered. What now appears on the screen?

options.A: A broad central bright band with weaker side bands; the close fringes vanish
options.B: The same fringes at half the brightness
options.C: A sharp image of the open slit with no spreading

r1.text: Fringes need two coherent sources; one slit alone gives only its own diffraction pattern.

r2.text: Each slit makes the fringes by itself, so one slit gives the same fringes with half the light.

r3.text: A narrow opening sends light in a narrow beam, so you see a thin line.

stem: Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through a single slit 0.10 mm wide onto a screen 2.0 m away. How wide is the central bright band?

r1.text: The central band runs from the first minimum on one side to the first on the other: 2 lambda D / a.

r2.text: The light keeps the width of the slit, so the band is as wide as the slit.

r3.text: With one opening the pattern is just a dimmer copy of the double-slit fringes.
